credit.credit-words: Although not technically a time signature, swing does influence the rhythm of the music so I'll cover it here.
Swing means that when seeing a written-out line in plain eighth notes (sometimes sixteenth notes) grouped in
pairs, the first note of each pair should be lengthened and the second one shortened somewhat. The precise
amount of lengthening and shortening is what gives a particular swing its feel, but to a first approximation it
Jazz and Funk are not the only types of music where this kind of modification happens. Folk music is full of this,
and there are even examples from the baroque and classical eras. In the baroque period there was a performance
technique called "Notes Inégales", very similar to swing, often indicated by slurring the long-short pairs of notes.
The Viennese Waltz from the classical period is performed with a very slight shortening of the first beat, so the
second beat arrives slightly early. This is known as "Schlepping." It's too subtle to be called a syncopation, and
it may come and go during a performance, sometimes being completely absent.

direction-type.words: A time signature is a pair of numbers, like a fraction, placed at the start of a bar or sequence of bars. The upper
number tells you how many beats in the bar, and the lower number tells you what kind of beat (quarter note, half
All the time signatures above, who's upper number is 2, 3 or 4 and who's lower number is a power of 2 are called
simple time signatures. There are many others, for example 4/8 (four eighth notes) 3/2 (three half notes) etc.
Beyond the simple time signatures are the compound ones. A compound time signature can be thought of as two
bars of a simple time signature. There is a good argument that 4/4 is a compound time signature because it can be
thought of as two bars of 2/4, but it is such a common time signature that it is usually put with the simple ones.
You can think of 6/8 as 2/4 with triplets. Other 6-beat time signatures are possible, for example 6/4 or even 6/2.
Irregular time signatures can not be divided into equal subdivisions.
Any irregular time signature can be built from a sequence of two and three beat components. People instinctively
break down these longer sequences of beats into groups of two and/or three. For example 5/8 can be counted as
three followed by two or two followed by three. There is no clear convention about metrenome markings for
irregular time signatures, You might consider using eighth notes for 5/8 but be aware that a real (clockwork)
metrenome can't go higher than around 208 bpm, and that's not particularily fast for eighth notes.
We skipped over 10/8 etc because 10/8 is, like 6/8, usually considered a compound time signature. 10/8 normally
means two bars of 5/8 with a weaker emphasis on the second bar. We'll say more about that in the next section.
So I'll stick my neck out and suggest that all properly irregular time signatures have a prime number of beats per
bar, greater than three: 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 etc. meaning they are not just a combination of two or more copies of a
It will probably have occurred to you that just as we can group the beats of irregular time signatures in different
ways, we could do the same with simple and compound time signatures. The most common example of this is
called a Hemiola rhythm, which alternates or superimposes bars of 3/4 and 6/8. A famous example of the
alternating form of a Hemiola is the song "America" from Leonard Bernstein's "West Side Story".
And let's not forget Dave Brubeck's "Blue Rondo a la Turk" - 9/8 as 3 bars of 2+2+2+3 and one bar of 3+3+3.
When layering different subdivisions, if the different rhythms are on different staves, it is sometimes clearer to
write two different time signatures at the same time.
Often a piece of music will not begin on the first beat of the bar. These extra notes before the first strong beat
are called an anacrusis (pronounced a-na-CRU-sis, plural anacruses) and any implied rests before the first and
last note are not written or played. It is also normal for the last bar to omit the beats that made up the anacrusis.
That final bar is called the complement.
Beyond this point the possibilities are effectively endless, though above a certain number of beats per bar it
becomes more practical to notate a rhythm as alternating simpler time signatures, it's just easier to read. Here's
a lovely English folk tune "Searching for Lambs" which alternates three bars of 5/4 with one bar of 3/4. I guess
you could notate it as 18/4, but it wouldn't be as easy to follow.
These are time signatures where the lower number is not a power of two, for example 4/3. They aren't as strange
as you might first think, and have some uses, but firstly what do they mean? Well if you read 4/4 as "four
quarters of a whole note", and 6/8 as "six eigths of a whole note" then it's obvious that 4/3 is just "four thirds of
a whole note". A third of a whole note is the same as one beat of a half note triplet, so irrational time signatures
are a new way of indicating a metric modulation, that is a change in speed that is some precise multiple of the
previous bar, and for that reason you would never begin a piece with an irrational time signature, but you might
change to them within a piece.
Let's pursue changing from 4/4 to 4/3 as an example. If a piece features half note triplets in 4/4 then indicating
4/3 says you want four quarter notes in the bar with each quarter note having the same duration as the triplet half
MuseScore doesn't support this type of time signature properly yet, you can create them but you still need to
add (and hide) a tempo change to make this play back correctly.
